# Assembling the Compendium {#sec-zzcollab} A collaborator clones your repository, runs the analysis script, and gets a p-value of 0.06 where your draft reports 0.04. Nothing errors. Over two days the two of you find three differences: her R packages are a year newer than yours, the cleaned dataset in the repository was produced by a version of the cleaning script you have since edited, and one exclusion was made by hand in a spreadsheet that never entered the repository. Each difference is a piece of the study that did not travel with the code. Pin the packages and the same rerun can still differ: if the repository could not hold the outcomes file and the README said to copy it from a shared drive that now holds a later, corrected extract, nothing in the repository could tell either of you that the inputs differed. A research compendium is the arrangement in which everything needed to produce the paper, from the raw data to the environment, lives in one directory with a layout a stranger can read, and the Five Pillars are the checklist that says every layer the answer depends on is pinned. This chapter sets out what a compendium is and where its files go, then assembles the pillars, builds the result, and audits it, so that the collaborator's rerun either matches or tells you why not. ::: {.bookepigraph} ```{=latex} \begin{flushright}\small ``` *We introduce the concept of a compendium as both a container for the different elements that make up the document and its computations (i.e. text, code, data, ...), and as a means for distributing, managing and updating the collection.* [Robert Gentleman and Duncan Temple Lang]{.smallcaps}, *Statistical Analyses and Reproducible Research* (2007) ```{=latex} \end{flushright} ``` ::: ::: {.column-margin} ![Robert Gentleman, co-creator of R and, with Duncan Temple Lang, author of the 2007 paper that introduced the research compendium this chapter builds on. Photograph by the R Consortium, [CC BY 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0/), via Wikimedia Commons.](images/portraits/gentleman.jpg){fig-alt='Portrait photograph of Robert Gentleman.'} ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Where this chapter sits: the compendium is what you share, the whole pipeline from raw data to report packaged so that someone else can rerun it, and its Five Pillars assemble the Environment band that runs under every stage.](10-zzcollab_files/figure-html/fig-zzcollab-pipeline-1.png){#fig-zzcollab-pipeline fig-align='center' fig-alt='Diagram of the analysis pipeline: six stages in order (Plan, Acquire, Wrangle, Analyze, Report, Share) above two bands that run under every stage (Version control and Environment). Highlighted for this chapter: Share and Environment.' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note title='In this chapter'} **Reading time.** About 35 minutes. **You'll need.** @sec-git-solo for commits and tags, @sec-quarto for the paper, @sec-renv for the lockfile, and @sec-docker for the container, in particular the canonical Dockerfile of @sec-docker-canonical. The code calls every function with its namespace (`purrr::walk()`, `renv::lockfile_read()`, `cli::hash_file_sha256()`), so it needs no `library()` call. **You'll be able to.** - Name the Five Pillars, what each pins, and the silent failure its absence causes, and say which a given repository lacks. - Place each file of a project in the conventional layout, and protect the raw data with a checksum manifest. - Assemble a compendium by hand from the `rrtools` layout (or a Quarto project), `renv`, the canonical Dockerfile, and the manifest, with the paper written inside it. - Audit a compendium against the pillars with a short script, and verify it by rebuilding it from a fresh clone. - Choose between assembling by hand and automating with `rrtools`, `workflowr`, or `zzcollab`, for a given project. **Outline.** - [What a research compendium is](#sec-rrtools) - [Where files go](#sec-rrtools-layout) - [The Five Pillars](#sec-zzcollab-pillars) - [Assembling the compendium by hand](#sec-zzcollab-assemble) - [Building and sharing](#sec-rrtools-build) - [Worked example: a small compendium](#sec-rrtools-worked) - [Auditing the pillars](#sec-zzcollab-audit) - [Choosing how much to automate](#sec-zzcollab-choosing) - [Optional: automating the assembly with zzcollab](#sec-zzcollab-optional) ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Skip ahead?'} If these answers come quickly, skip to the next chapter. The answers are in @sec-quiz-answers-10. 1. What is a 'research compendium' as described by Marwick, Boettiger, and Mullen (2018) [@marwick2018packaging], and how does an `rrtools` compendium differ from a regular R package? 2. What are the *Five Pillars* of a reproducible research compendium? A project has a committed `renv.lock` and a Dockerfile: which pillars does it still lack, and how would anyone notice? 3. When is a framework such as `rrtools`, `workflowr`, or `zzcollab` worth adopting, and what does it leave for you to do? ::: ## What a research compendium is {#sec-rrtools} A paper without its compendium is a description of an analysis; a compendium without a paper is code. Together they are a study artifact that survives the loss of any individual file, and of any individual person. Gentleman and Temple Lang [-@gentleman2007statistical] introduced the term, and Marwick, Boettiger, and Mullen [-@marwick2018packaging] gave the working definition this book uses, which has three criteria: | Criterion | What it requires | What fails without it | |---|---|---| | Single directory | Code, data, environment, and narrative together | A step lives elsewhere (a spreadsheet, a laptop), as the hand exclusion in the opening did | | Computable | Another user can rerun the analysis with reasonable effort | The paper can be read but not checked | | Self-describing | The layout follows a convention a stranger knows | Every file is a hunt, for the stranger and for you in eighteen months | : The three criteria for a research compendium. {#tbl-rrtools-criteria} The argument for convention is practical. A directory organized to your own logic is navigable by you and by nobody else, and 'nobody else' includes the version of you that returns after eighteen months. A compendium that follows a recognized layout can be opened by a stranger who has seen one before: they will know where the paper is, where the raw data are, and which directory holds things that were derived rather than given. The specific convention matters much less than having one at all. R packages already have a convention every R user knows (`DESCRIPTION`, `R/`, `man/`), which satisfies the third criterion and part of the first. What a package lacks is a study: data and a paper. The `rrtools` package [@marwick2018rrtools] supplies one convention that adds them, and @fig-compendium-anatomy shows the result. ```{mermaid} %%| echo: false %%| label: fig-compendium-anatomy %%| fig-alt: "Flowchart. A research compendium branches into three %%| components: a package backbone of DESCRIPTION, R/ and man/; %%| an analysis directory holding data, paper and figures; and a %%| Dockerfile with renv.lock. Each leads in turn to the property %%| it supplies: self-describing so a stranger can navigate it, a %%| single directory holding code, data and narrative together, %%| and computable so another user can re-run it." %%| fig-cap: "What a compendium is made of. The package backbone %%| supplies convention and dependency declaration; the analysis %%| directory supplies the study; the Dockerfile supplies the %%| environment. Remove any of the three and the reader loses %%| navigability, content, or the ability to run it." flowchart TD C["Research compendium"] C --> P["Package backbone
DESCRIPTION, R/, man/
convention and dependencies"] C --> A["analysis/
data/, paper/, figures/
the study itself"] C --> D["Dockerfile + renv.lock
the environment"] P --> N["self-describing
a stranger can navigate it"] A --> S["single directory
code, data, narrative together"] D --> R["computable
another user can re-run it"] ``` ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** Why does `rrtools` reuse the R package structure instead of inventing a new layout? **Answer.** Three practical reasons. The package structure is the only widely recognized layout in the R ecosystem, so the compendium is navigable for free. The package gives dependency declaration: `DESCRIPTION` lists what the code needs, and `renv` (@sec-renv) pins the versions. And it gives function management: helpers in `R/` are documented, tested, and loadable into the analysis. The cost is a few package files that are not used as a package (no CRAN, the Comprehensive R Archive Network, submission, no users importing it), which is small against the structural payoff. ::: ## Where files go {#sec-rrtools-layout} ### The layout `rrtools` produces the layout below; most compendium conventions differ from it only in names. ``` readmissions/ ├── DESCRIPTION ├── NAMESPACE ├── R/ # reusable functions ├── man/ ├── analysis/ │ ├── data/ │ │ ├── raw_data/ │ │ └── derived_data/ │ ├── figures/ │ ├── paper/ │ │ ├── paper.qmd │ │ └── references.bib │ └── supplementary-materials/ ├── Dockerfile ├── data-manifest.sha256 ├── .github/ │ └── workflows/ ├── README.qmd ├── README.md └── readmissions.Rproj ``` | Path | Holds | Commit it? | |---|---|---| | `R/` | Reusable functions: cleaning helpers, plotting wrappers, model utilities, documented with roxygen | Yes | | `analysis/data/raw_data/` | The data exactly as received, never edited | If small and unrestricted; otherwise document the access path | | `analysis/data/derived_data/` | Everything the scripts produce from the raw data | Optional: commit when small and the analysis is archived | | `analysis/paper/paper.qmd` | The manuscript, with the code that produces its numbers | Yes | | `analysis/figures/` | Figures the analysis writes | Usually not; the code that makes them is committed | | `analysis/supplementary-materials/` | Appendix tables, sensitivity analyses | Yes | | `data-manifest.sha256` | One checksum per raw file | Yes, always, even when the raw data cannot be committed | | `README.qmd` | What the project is, how to build it in one command, where the paper and data are, how to cite it | Yes | : Where each file goes. {#tbl-rrtools-layout} The README is the entry point, not the documentation: it says what the project is, how to rebuild it, and where things are. Long technical notes live elsewhere. ### Raw data are read-only Raw and derived data live in separate directories because raw data are evidence and derived data are a build product. Writing a cleaned table back over the input destroys the only copy of what you were given, and version control does not recover a file that was overwritten before it was ever committed. Treat `raw_data/` as read-only, by convention if your file system will not enforce it, and make the convention checkable: record a checksum of every raw file when it arrives. The chunk below builds the layout above in a temporary directory and copies in two of the HF-HOME raw files. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} comp <- file.path(tempdir(), "readmissions") layout <- c("R", "analysis/data/raw_data", "analysis/data/derived_data", "analysis/paper", "analysis/figures") purrr::walk(file.path(comp, layout), dir.create, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE) hf_dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw_data", "hfhome") raw_dir <- file.path(comp, "analysis", "data", "raw_data") file.copy(file.path(hf_dir, c("randomization.csv", "outcomes.csv")), raw_dir, overwrite = TRUE) #> [1] TRUE TRUE ``` ::: The manifest is one line per file: the file's SHA-256 checksum (a 64-character fingerprint of its contents) and its path from the compendium root, in the format the `shasum` command reads and writes, so that you can create it in R and anyone can check it from a shell. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} raw_files <- list.files(raw_dir, pattern = "\\.csv$") sums <- vapply(file.path(raw_dir, raw_files), cli::hash_file_sha256, character(1)) writeLines(paste0(sums, " ", file.path("analysis", "data", "raw_data", raw_files)), file.path(comp, "data-manifest.sha256")) readLines(file.path(comp, "data-manifest.sha256")) #> [1] "8746dd3588f207193182c3499ae588c255e567d99d374ea5650da1e5f974f7c4 analysis/data/raw_data/outcomes.csv" #> [2] "118b64fe01fd38f25777ee6731b78e9c8a1038781fa12bd4ac4fbe3c7d261e88 analysis/data/raw_data/randomization.csv" check_raw <- function(root) { lines <- readLines(file.path(root, "data-manifest.sha256")) recorded <- setNames(sub(" .*$", "", lines), sub("^\\S+ ", "", lines)) current <- vapply(file.path(root, names(recorded)), cli::hash_file_sha256, character(1)) changed <- names(recorded)[unname(current) != recorded] if (length(changed) > 0) { stop("raw data changed since the manifest: ", paste(changed, collapse = ", "), call. = FALSE) } invisible(TRUE) } check_raw(comp) ``` ::: From the compendium root, `shasum -a 256 --check data-manifest.sha256` checks the same manifest from the shell. A checksum detects accidental change, which is the job here; it is not a defense against deliberate tampering, since whoever can edit the data can edit the manifest beside them. ::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'} **A 'quick fix' saved over the raw export leaves no trace in the data.** Exclude a few patients by hand and save the file in place, and every later run reads the edited file as if it were what the site sent: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} outcomes_path <- file.path(raw_dir, "outcomes.csv") outcomes <- read.csv(outcomes_path, colClasses = c(patient_id = "character")) write.csv(outcomes[-(1:3), ], outcomes_path, row.names = FALSE) check_raw(comp) #> Error: #> ! raw data changed since the manifest: analysis/data/raw_data/outcomes.csv ``` ::: The analysis would have run, on 2,429 patients instead of 2,432, with no error. The manifest makes it loud. Exclusions belong in code, in `derived_data/`, where they are counted and reviewed. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** Your cleaning script reads `analysis/data/raw_data/visits.csv` and produces a tidy analytic table. Where does the output go, and should it be committed? **Answer.** It goes in `analysis/data/derived_data/`, and whether to commit it is a trade-off, not a rule. Against committing: it is reproducible from the raw data and the script, so storing it duplicates information and adds a binary that changes on every run. For committing: it lets a reader check your numbers without installing your environment, and it fixes what the analysis actually used, which matters if the cleaning script is later corrected. The usual resolution is to commit derived data when it is small and the analysis is being archived, and to leave it untracked during development. What is not defensible is committing derived data and *not* the script that made it, which is the arrangement that looks tidiest and explains least, and the one behind the opening's stale dataset. ::: ### Exercises 1. Assign each file from a messy project to the layout of @tbl-rrtools-layout: `helpers.R` (three functions used by two scripts), `crf_export_2025-06-01.csv` (from the data center), `analytic.rds` (written by `clean.R`), `fig2.png`, `notes.txt` (a dated log of decisions), `clean.R`, and `manuscript.qmd`. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} | File | Goes to | Why | |---|---|---| | `helpers.R` | `R/` | Reused by more than one script | | `crf_export_2025-06-01.csv` | `analysis/data/raw_data/` | Received, not produced; add it to the manifest | | `analytic.rds` | `analysis/data/derived_data/` | Produced by a script; regenerable | | `fig2.png` | `analysis/figures/` (usually untracked) | Produced by code | | `notes.txt` | Top level or `analysis/` as a decision log | Not data and not code; keep it with the project and in Git | | `clean.R` | `analysis/` (scripts) | Study-specific code that turns raw into derived data | | `manuscript.qmd` | `analysis/paper/paper.qmd` | The manuscript | The judgment calls are `notes.txt`, which fits no category and should not be forced into one, and `clean.R`, which some conventions put in `analysis/scripts/`. What matters is that a stranger can predict the location. ::: ## The Five Pillars {#sec-zzcollab-pillars} The three criteria say what a compendium must achieve, and the layout says where its files go. The Five Pillars say what it must contain to achieve them. The preceding chapters each solved one layer of the reproducibility problem and each left the wiring to you. A compendium layout does not come with a lockfile; a lockfile (@sec-renv) does not come with a container; a container (@sec-docker) does not know where your data came from. The Five Pillars are the checklist that says when the wiring is complete. They are tool-neutral roles: the book uses the R tools for each, but every language has a tool for each role, and the same five hold whether you assemble them by hand or let a framework do it. @tbl-five-pillars states what each pins and what goes wrong without it. | Pillar | Pins | In this book | Elsewhere | Without it | Check | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | 1. Dockerfile | Operating system, system libraries, the R build | `Dockerfile` (@sec-docker) | Apptainer definition, Nix | Packages restore onto a different R or BLAS (Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms), and the last digits of an estimate move | The base image's R version equals the lockfile's | | 2. `renv.lock` | The exact version and source of every R package | `renv.lock` (@sec-renv) | `uv.lock`, conda `environment.yml` | A collaborator's newer packages, or a changed default in one, change a number without an error | `renv::status()` reports no issues | | 3. `.Rprofile` | Activation of the project library at startup | `.Rprofile` (@sec-renv) | A virtual-environment activation script | R loads the global library instead, and the lockfile is silently bypassed | `.libPaths()[1]` is inside `renv/library` where you render | | 4. Source code | Every step, from raw data to every number | `R/` and `analysis/` in Git (@sec-git-solo) | Any version-controlled scripts | A hand step or an edited script is not in the history, or nobody can identify the version that ran | Committed to Git, and the submitted version tagged | | 5. Data | The raw inputs, unchanged, or the documented way to get them | `analysis/data/raw_data/` with a checksum manifest | A DOI'd deposit with access instructions | A stale derived file or a later extract gives a different answer from the same code | A committed checksum manifest verifies | : The Five Pillars as a tool-neutral checklist. Each is necessary; none is sufficient, and a compendium missing any one is incomplete. {#tbl-five-pillars} The opening's three causes map onto pillars 2, 4, and 5. The remedy for each is not care but a file: a lockfile, a script for every step, and raw data that the code reads and never writes. Some frameworks automate the pillars; `zzcollab` (@sec-zzcollab-optional) is one, and it scaffolds and audits all five. The pillars are easier to remember as a stack than as a list, because each one captures a layer the one above it takes for granted. @fig-five-pillars is that stack. ```{mermaid} %%| echo: false %%| label: fig-five-pillars %%| fig-alt: "Five layers stacked bottom to top, each depending on %%| the one below. From the bottom: the Dockerfile supplying %%| operating system, system libraries and the R build; renv.lock %%| pinning every R package version; .Rprofile activating the %%| project library; the source code in R/ and analysis/; and at %%| the top the data, raw and derived or a documented path to %%| it." %%| fig-cap: "The Five Pillars as a layered stack. Each layer %%| assumes the one beneath it. Remove the Dockerfile and the R %%| packages have no operating system to install onto; remove the %%| lockfile and the source code has no packages; remove the data %%| and there is nothing to analyze." flowchart TD D["5. Data
raw and derived, or a documented path to them"] S["4. Source code
the analysis, in R/ and analysis/"] P["3. .Rprofile
activates the project library"] L["2. renv.lock
every R package version"] F["1. Dockerfile
operating system, system libraries, R build"] F --> L --> P --> S --> D ``` Two of the pillars need a word more than the table gives them. The `renv.lock` records the R version as well as every package, but it does not install R; the R installation comes from the Dockerfile, which is why the two must agree. And the data pillar does not require the data to be in the repository. Sensitive data often cannot live in the compendium; then the compendium holds a README documenting the access path, in the form @sec-federal sets out, and a manifest of checksums that lets anyone confirm they obtained the same files. The shared-drive variant of the opening was a data pillar with the README and without the manifest. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** A project has a Dockerfile and a committed `renv.lock`, and its `.Rprofile` activates `renv`. Which pillars does a collaborator still have to take on trust? **Answer.** Two. The source code is pinned only if it is committed and the version you reported is tagged; otherwise the collaborator cannot know which commit produced the paper. And the data are pinned only if they are in the repository or a manifest records their checksums; otherwise a later extract produces a different answer from the same code, with nothing to say so. The environment pillars cannot detect either problem. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** Your compendium has a `renv.lock` and a Dockerfile. A colleague argues that the lockfile is redundant, because the image already contains the packages. Is it? **Answer.** No. The image contains the packages that were current when it was built, and a rebuild months later installs whatever is current then, unless the lockfile pins them; the Dockerfile's restore step reads the lockfile for exactly that reason. The pillars are a stack, not a menu: the Dockerfile pins what is beneath R, and the lockfile pins what is above it. ::: ### Exercises 2. A repository contains `analysis.R`, `clean.R`, `data.csv` (described in the README as 'cleaned'), `renv.lock`, and a README that says 'run analysis.R in RStudio'. Which pillars are present, which are missing, and what would a collaborator's rerun be unable to establish? ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} Present: package versions (`renv.lock`) and source code, assuming the repository is under Git. Missing: the environment beneath R (no Dockerfile, so R and system libraries are whatever the collaborator has), activation (no `.Rprofile`, so the lockfile is ignored unless she restores it by hand), and the raw data. The data pillar is the serious gap: `data.csv` is derived, so a rerun can check `analysis.R` against it but can never check `clean.R`, and any hand step between the raw export and `data.csv` is invisible. Add the raw export (or its access path), make `clean.R` read it and write to `derived_data/`, and record a checksum manifest. ::: ## Assembling the compendium by hand {#sec-zzcollab-assemble} Assembling the pillars by hand takes about half an hour per project, and doing it once is the best way to understand what any framework that automates it is doing for you. Each step uses a tool from an earlier chapter; the commands below are display-only, because they create a project on your machine. 1. **Layout and source code.** Scaffold the compendium with `rrtools` (@sec-rrtools-scaffold) and put it under Git (@sec-git-solo): ```r rrtools::use_compendium("~/research/hfhome") rrtools::use_analysis() ``` ```bash git init ``` 2. **Lockfile and `.Rprofile`.** Initialize `renv`, which writes both, install what the analysis uses, and snapshot (@sec-renv): ```r renv::init() renv::snapshot() ``` 3. **Dockerfile.** Copy the canonical Dockerfile from @sec-docker-canonical to the project root, with its `.dockerignore`, and set the base image's tag to the R version in `renv.lock`. Use it in place of the one `rrtools::use_dockerfile()` writes (@sec-rrtools-scaffold). 4. **Data.** Put the raw files in `analysis/data/raw_data/`, or a README there that says how to obtain them, and commit a checksum manifest of the files (@sec-rrtools-layout). 5. **Tag.** Commit, and tag the commit you submit: ```bash git tag -a v1.0-submission -m "Submitted to journal" ``` ### Scaffolding with `rrtools` {#sec-rrtools-scaffold} The calls below are display-only, because they create a project and open it as a new RStudio session: ```r # install install.packages("remotes") remotes::install_github("benmarwick/rrtools") # create a new compendium rrtools::use_compendium("~/research/readmissions") # (this also runs usethis::create_package internally) # add the analysis directories rrtools::use_analysis() # add a Dockerfile and, by default, a GitHub Actions # workflow that renders the paper inside it rrtools::use_dockerfile() # add a README.qmd rrtools::use_readme_qmd() ``` `rrtools::use_dockerfile()` writes its own Dockerfile, based on `rocker/verse`. This book replaces it with the canonical Dockerfile in @sec-rrtools-build, so that this chapter, @sec-renv, and @sec-docker describe one file rather than several. ### Other conventions `rrtools` is one convention among several, and the right one depends on the project's shape and the team's habits: | Convention | Shape | Use when | |---|---|---| | `rrtools` | R package plus `analysis/` | A paper with reusable R code; the default for a biostatistical paper | | Quarto manuscript project | A Quarto project whose output is an article | A paper-first project without a package backbone | | Quarto book | A Quarto project with chapters | Book-length output, such as this practicum | | A framework such as `zzcollab` (@sec-zzcollab-optional) | Scaffolds all five pillars and audits them | You want the pillars generated and checked for you | | The TIER Protocol (Teaching Integrity in Empirical Research) | A documented folder convention | Social-science collaborators who already use it | | Your group's template | Whatever the group agreed | Always, if one exists: consistency with colleagues beats any external default | : Compendium conventions. {#tbl-rrtools-conventions} Defaulting to `rrtools` is reasonable; defaulting to it without thought is not. ::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'} Use a model to propose a layout for an existing project, and apply the moves yourself. > **Context.** Below is the output of `git ls-files` for an R > analysis project, and the compendium layout I want (the table of > paths and contents). The working tree is clean and committed. > > **Constraints.** Propose only `git mv` commands. Do not move, > rename, or edit anything under `data/raw/`; raw files keep their > names and contents, and are moved, if at all, only into > `analysis/data/raw_data/` with a separate command I will run > myself. Delete nothing. Do not edit file contents. > > **Criteria.** Every file is assigned exactly once. List the > files that fit no category, with your reasoning, rather than > forcing them into one, and list every script whose file paths > will break after the moves. *Failure mode.* A model assigns every file somewhere, confidently, including logs and exploratory notebooks that fit nowhere, and proposes edits to paths inside scripts that silently change what they read. Raw files moved or renamed lose the link to their provenance. *Check.* After applying the moves, `git status` and `git diff -M --name-status HEAD` should show only renames (`R100`), no modifications or deletions; `shasum -a 256 --check data-manifest.sha256`, rerun after the manifest's paths are updated to the new locations, should pass; and a fresh render should produce the same numbers. The prompt sends file names, not data (@sec-ai-governance). ::: ### The paper inside the compendium {#sec-rrtools-paper} `analysis/paper/paper.qmd` is the manuscript, written in Quarto (@sec-quarto): code chunks for the analyses, inline numbers, figure cross-references, and citations from `references.bib`. ````qmd --- title: "Effect of post-discharge home health visits on 30-day readmission" author: - name: A. Author - name: B. Coauthor format: pdf: default html: default bibliography: references.bib --- # Methods We analyzed `{{r}} nrow(d)` patients from the institutional EHR cohort. The primary outcome was 30-day all-cause readmission and the exposure was receipt of a home-health visit. We fit a multivariable logistic regression adjusting for age, sex, baseline ejection fraction, and discharge medications, in R [@rcore2024]. ```{{r}} #| label: fit-model #| echo: false fit <- glm(readmit ~ home_health + age + sex + ef + meds, family = binomial, data = d) ci <- exp(confint.default(fit)["home_health", ]) ``` The adjusted odds ratio for home-health-visit receipt was `{{r}} round(exp(coef(fit)["home_health"]), 2)` (95% CI `{{r}} round(ci[1], 2)` to `{{r}} round(ci[2], 2)`). ```` Every number in the methods and results comes from code, so a rerun on corrected data changes the prose with the tables. EHR here is the electronic health record; the example is an observational cohort, which is why the exposure is receipt of a visit and the estimate is adjusted. For journal-specific formatting in Quarto, use a Quarto journal extension where one exists for your journal. The `quarto-journals` collection on GitHub includes, for example, a template for JASA (the *Journal of the American Statistical Association*): ```bash quarto use template quarto-journals/jasa ``` The extension adds a format (here `jasa-pdf`) that you name under `format:` in `paper.qmd`. The older `rticles` package offers more journals, including *Statistics in Medicine*, *Biometrics*, and JASA (`rticles::journals()` lists them), but its templates are R Markdown output formats for an `.Rmd` file rendered with `rmarkdown::render()`, not Quarto formats; they cannot be named in the `format:` key of a `.qmd`. Neither collection has a template for every medical journal (there is none for NEJM or JAMA, for instance), and most of those journals accept a plain PDF or Word manuscript at first submission. ::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'} Render the paper in a fresh session and read the warnings, which are where unresolved citations and cross-references surface: ```bash quarto render analysis/paper/paper.qmd 2>&1 | grep -i warn ``` It should print nothing. A warning that a citation or a cross-reference cannot be resolved means the rendered paper shows a placeholder where a reference belongs. ::: ### A compendium with two gaps The manifest is the step most projects skip. The chunk below assembles a small HF-HOME compendium in a temporary directory, with the manifest step deliberately left out and a Dockerfile copied from an older project, so that the audit in @sec-zzcollab-audit has something to find. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} hf_dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw_data", "hfhome") comp <- file.path(tempdir(), "hfhome-compendium") unlink(comp, recursive = TRUE) raw <- file.path(comp, "analysis", "data", "raw_data") dir.create(raw, recursive = TRUE) dir.create(file.path(comp, "R")) invisible(file.copy( file.path(hf_dir, c("randomization.csv", "outcomes.csv")), raw )) writeLines( "derive_analysis_set <- function(rand, outc) merge(rand, outc)", file.path(comp, "R", "derive.R") ) writeLines('source("renv/activate.R")', file.path(comp, ".Rprofile")) writeLines( '{"R": {"Version": "4.4.0", "Repositories": []}, "Packages": {}}', file.path(comp, "renv.lock") ) writeLines(c("FROM rocker/r-ver:4.3.1", "WORKDIR /work"), file.path(comp, "Dockerfile")) invisible(system2("git", c("init", "-q", comp))) list.files(comp, recursive = TRUE, all.files = TRUE, include.dirs = FALSE) |> grep(pattern = "^[.]git/", invert = TRUE, value = TRUE) #> [1] ".Rprofile" #> [2] "analysis/data/raw_data/outcomes.csv" #> [3] "analysis/data/raw_data/randomization.csv" #> [4] "Dockerfile" #> [5] "R/derive.R" #> [6] "renv.lock" ``` ::: Every pillar has a file. Whether every pillar is *pinned* is a different question, and the listing cannot answer it. ::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'} **An `.Rprofile` that never runs.** R reads `.Rprofile` from the directory it starts in, then from your home directory. Render from a subdirectory (`cd analysis/paper`, or an RStudio project rooted there) and the project's `.Rprofile` at the root never runs: no error, no message, and the analysis uses your global library while the lockfile says otherwise. This book hit exactly this, because Quarto starts R in the directory being rendered; its fix is a second `.Rprofile` in `analysis/report/` that points `renv` at the project root. The check in @tbl-five-pillars catches it: run `.libPaths()[1]` from the directory where you render. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** Step 3 sets the Dockerfile's base tag to the R version in `renv.lock`. What happens if the two disagree, and why is nothing likely to report it? **Answer.** `renv` restores the recorded package versions onto whatever R the image supplies. The build usually succeeds, because most package versions install on a neighboring R, and the analysis runs. What changes is the layer beneath the packages (R itself, and the numerical libraries it links), so results can differ in their last digits from the ones you reported, with no error anywhere. ::: ## Building and sharing {#sec-rrtools-build} A compendium is built in one of three ways: render the paper in RStudio while writing; source the analysis scripts in order after `devtools::load_all()` to regenerate cached results; or build the image, which is the only one that reproduces the environment as well as the results. The book's canonical Dockerfile, explained line by line in @sec-docker-canonical, sits at the compendium root: ```dockerfile # syntax=docker/dockerfile:1 FROM rocker/r-ver:4.4.0 ARG QUARTO_VERSION=1.6.40 RUN apt-get update \ && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \ ca-certificates curl \ libcurl4-openssl-dev libssl-dev libxml2-dev libuv1-dev \ && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* # rocker/r-ver ships R but not the Quarto CLI RUN arch="$(dpkg --print-architecture)" \ && curl -fsSL -o /tmp/quarto.deb \ "https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/releases/download/v${QUARTO_VERSION}/quarto-${QUARTO_VERSION}-linux-${arch}.deb" \ && dpkg -i /tmp/quarto.deb \ && rm /tmp/quarto.deb # outside /work, so a bind mount of the project cannot hide it ENV RENV_PATHS_LIBRARY=/opt/renv/library WORKDIR /work COPY renv.lock .Rprofile ./ COPY renv/activate.R renv/activate.R RUN R -q -e "renv::restore(prompt = FALSE)" COPY . . CMD ["quarto", "render", "analysis/paper/paper.qmd"] ``` From the compendium root (display-only): ```bash docker build --platform linux/amd64 -t readmissions:v1.0 . docker run --rm --platform linux/amd64 \ -v "$(pwd)/analysis/paper:/work/analysis/paper" \ readmissions:v1.0 ``` The Dockerfile pins the R version, the system libraries, and (through `renv.lock`) the package versions, and the rendered paper appears in `analysis/paper/` on your machine. A reader with Docker can rebuild a very close copy of the environment that produced the paper; an exact copy needs the digest pin or archived image described in @sec-docker. Deposition is treated in full in @sec-federal. Its shape affects how you organize the directory, so it is worth knowing now: GitHub (or your institution's Git server) holds the working repository; an archive such as Zenodo holds a citable, DOI-bearing (digital object identifier) snapshot at submission, with the saved image; and restricted primary data go only where the data use agreement permits, often a controlled-access repository and sometimes nowhere, with the compendium documenting how to request them. ::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'} The test of a compendium is a rebuild by someone who is not you, from what is in the repository and nothing else. Simulate it (display-only): ```bash git clone https://github.com/you/readmissions.git /tmp/fresh cd /tmp/fresh docker build --platform linux/amd64 -t readmissions:check . docker run --rm --platform linux/amd64 \ -v "$(pwd)/analysis/paper:/work/analysis/paper" readmissions:check ``` The paper must render, and its key numbers must match yours. A failure here names a file that lives only on your machine, which is the opening's problem found before your collaborator finds it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** Why is the fresh clone the right test, rather than rendering the paper again on your own machine? **Answer.** Your machine has everything the repository forgot: the packages you installed, the derived files you never committed, the environment variables in your `.Renviron`. A rerun there passes whatever the compendium is missing. A fresh clone, built in a container, has only what the five pillars supply, so it is the first run that can fail for the reasons a collaborator's would. ::: ### Exercises 3. A colleague's compendium renders on her laptop and fails in the fresh-clone check with `cannot open file 'analysis/data/derived_data/analytic.rds'`. What is the likely cause, and what are the two acceptable fixes? ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} The paper reads a derived file that exists on her disk and is not in the repository, probably because `derived_data/` is listed in `.gitignore` and nothing in the build regenerates it. Either make the build produce it (the paper, or a script the Dockerfile's command runs, calls the cleaning code on the raw data), which is the better fix because it also tests the cleaning; or commit the derived file together with the script that made it, which is acceptable for an archived analysis. Committing it without the script is the arrangement the layout Check warned against. ::: ## Worked example: a small compendium {#sec-rrtools-worked} A simulation study set up as a compendium from scratch (display-only): ```r # scaffold; this opens the new compendium as its own # RStudio project, and every later call runs in that # session, whose working directory is the compendium rrtools::use_compendium("~/research/sim2026") rrtools::use_analysis() rrtools::use_readme_qmd() # the environment pillars: initialize renv, then replace # rrtools's Dockerfile with the canonical one renv::init() # add the simulation function usethis::use_r("simulate") # (write R/simulate.R with a documented function) devtools::document() # add the paper file.edit("analysis/paper/paper.qmd") # (write the manuscript using simulate() from the package) # render quarto::quarto_render("analysis/paper/paper.qmd") # version control usethis::use_git() usethis::use_github(private = TRUE) ``` Then snapshot, commit, and tag the milestone from the shell, in the compendium directory: ```bash Rscript -e 'renv::snapshot()' git add . git commit -m "Initial compendium" git tag -a v0.1-draft -m "Initial draft for PI review" ``` The compendium is now a self-contained directory with package-style code, a paper that uses the code, a lockfile and a Dockerfile that pin the environment, a Git history, and a tag at a meaningful milestone. The setup takes about thirty minutes. ::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'} Confirm that the pillars are committed and the tree is clean: ```bash git ls-files Dockerfile renv.lock .Rprofile analysis/paper/paper.qmd git status --short git tag -l 'v0.1*' ``` The first command should list all four files, the second should print nothing, and the third should print `v0.1-draft`. Then run the fresh-clone check of @sec-rrtools-build against the tag. ::: ## Auditing the pillars {#sec-zzcollab-audit} A checklist you run by eye drifts; a checklist you run as code does not. The function below turns @tbl-five-pillars into five assertions about a project directory. It uses only `renv`, `cli`, and base R, so it audits a compendium however it was assembled. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} audit_pillars <- function(root) { path <- function(...) file.path(root, ...) lock_r <- if (file.exists(path("renv.lock"))) { renv::lockfile_read(path("renv.lock"))$R$Version } else { NA_character_ } from <- if (file.exists(path("Dockerfile"))) { grep("^FROM ", readLines(path("Dockerfile")), value = TRUE)[1] } else { NA_character_ } rprofile <- if (file.exists(path(".Rprofile"))) { readLines(path(".Rprofile")) } else { character(0) } code <- list.files(root, pattern = "[.](R|qmd|Rmd)$", recursive = TRUE) manifest <- path("data-manifest.sha256") data_ok <- file.exists(manifest) && { m <- read.table(manifest, col.names = c("sha256", "file")) all(vapply(path(m$file), cli::hash_file_sha256, character(1)) == m$sha256) } data.frame( pillar = c("Dockerfile", "renv.lock", ".Rprofile", "Source code", "Data"), check = c("base image tag equals the lockfile's R version", "lockfile present and readable", "activates renv", "analysis code present, under Git", "raw files match the checksum manifest"), ok = c( !is.na(from) && !is.na(lock_r) && grepl(paste0(":", lock_r, "($|@)"), from), !is.na(lock_r), any(grepl("renv/activate.R", rprofile, fixed = TRUE)), length(code) > 0 && file.exists(path(".git")), data_ok ) ) } audit_pillars(comp) #> pillar check ok #> 1 Dockerfile base image tag equals the lockfile's R version FALSE #> 2 renv.lock lockfile present and readable TRUE #> 3 .Rprofile activates renv TRUE #> 4 Source code analysis code present, under Git TRUE #> 5 Data raw files match the checksum manifest FALSE ``` ::: Two pillars fail. The Dockerfile names R 4.3.1 while the lockfile records 4.4.0, and there is no manifest for the data. Fix both: set the base tag to the lockfile's version, and write the manifest. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} lock_r <- renv::lockfile_read(file.path(comp, "renv.lock"))$R$Version writeLines(c(paste0("FROM rocker/r-ver:", lock_r), "WORKDIR /work"), file.path(comp, "Dockerfile")) data_files <- list.files(raw, full.names = TRUE) writeLines( paste0(vapply(data_files, cli::hash_file_sha256, character(1)), " ", file.path("analysis", "data", "raw_data", basename(data_files))), file.path(comp, "data-manifest.sha256") ) audit <- audit_pillars(comp) audit #> pillar check ok #> 1 Dockerfile base image tag equals the lockfile's R version TRUE #> 2 renv.lock lockfile present and readable TRUE #> 3 .Rprofile activates renv TRUE #> 4 Source code analysis code present, under Git TRUE #> 5 Data raw files match the checksum manifest TRUE ``` ::: ::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'} Assert the audit rather than reading it, and confirm from a shell that the manifest is in the standard format (display-only; run it in the compendium's root): ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} stopifnot(all(audit$ok)) ``` ::: ```bash shasum -a 256 --check data-manifest.sha256 ``` The shell check prints `OK` beside each file. In your own project, run `audit_pillars(".")` from the root before every tag, and regenerate the manifest only when you deliberately receive new data, committing it with the data change. For a project under Git, `git ls-files Dockerfile renv.lock .Rprofile` confirms that the files are committed, not merely present on your disk. ::: The audit is a structural check. It confirms that each pillar is present and consistent; it finds what is missing, and it cannot tell you that what is present works or that the analysis reproduces. That test is the rebuild from a fresh clone in @sec-rrtools-build: build the image, restore the lockfile, run the analysis, and compare the results with the ones you reported. ::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'} A model can map an unfamiliar project onto the pillars quickly. Give it the files that decide each pillar, not a description. > **Context.** Below are the output of > `git ls-files` for an R analysis project, the `FROM` line of its > Dockerfile, the `R$Version` from its `renv.lock`, and the full > text of its `.Rprofile`. > > **Constraints.** Assess the Five Pillars (Dockerfile, > `renv.lock`, `.Rprofile`, source code, data) using only these > inputs. Do not recommend a framework or a template. Do not > propose moving or editing anything in the raw-data directory. > > **Criteria.** For each pillar: present, absent, or present but > inert, with the line of input that shows it. For each gap, the > smallest addition that closes it. *Failure mode.* Models report a pillar as present because a file with the right name exists: an `.Rprofile` that never activates `renv`, a Dockerfile whose tag disagrees with the lockfile, a data README with no checksums. Or they recommend adopting a framework, which answers a different question. *Check.* Run `audit_pillars()` on the project and compare its `ok` column with the model's verdicts. File names and configuration are structure; send no data files (@sec-ai-governance). ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** The audit passes on your compendium. A month later a colleague edits one value in `outcomes.csv` to correct a data entry error and reruns the analysis. What does the audit report, and what should happen next? **Answer.** The data pillar fails, because the file's checksum no longer matches the manifest. That is the audit doing its job: the inputs changed, and now someone knows. Raw data are evidence, so the correction should arrive as a new extract with its provenance recorded, the manifest regenerated and committed with it, and the changed result explained, not as a hand edit to the file. ::: ### Exercises 4. In the toy compendium, change one outcome in `analysis/data/raw_data/outcomes.csv` and rerun the audit. Which pillar fails? ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} outcomes_path <- file.path(raw, "outcomes.csv") lines <- readLines(outcomes_path) lines[2] <- sub(",0,", ",1,", lines[2], fixed = TRUE) writeLines(lines, outcomes_path) audit_pillars(comp)[c("pillar", "ok")] #> pillar ok #> 1 Dockerfile TRUE #> 2 renv.lock TRUE #> 3 .Rprofile TRUE #> 4 Source code TRUE #> 5 Data FALSE ``` ::: Only the data pillar fails. A one-character change to one patient is invisible to every other check, and to anyone reading the results; the manifest is what makes it loud. ::: 5. Audit this book's own repository with `audit_pillars(file.path("..", ".."))` and explain each failure. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} audit_pillars(file.path("..", ".."))[c("pillar", "ok")] #> pillar ok #> 1 Dockerfile FALSE #> 2 renv.lock TRUE #> 3 .Rprofile TRUE #> 4 Source code TRUE #> 5 Data FALSE ``` ::: Each `FALSE` is a pillar the book's repository does not supply in the form the audit checks. A missing Dockerfile means the R version and system libraries are whatever the reader's machine has; a missing data manifest means the reader cannot confirm the files match the ones the book was built from, though here the HF-HOME files can be regenerated from their seeded script. A book that teaches the pillars is held to them too. ::: ## Choosing how much to automate {#sec-zzcollab-choosing} Assembling by hand gives you full control and costs half an hour per project. It is also exactly the kind of work that gets done slightly differently every time, which defeats the consistency it was supposed to produce. Alfred North Whitehead observed, in *An Introduction to Mathematics* (1911), that 'civilization advances by extending the number of important operations which we can perform without thinking about them'; the tools below make the assembly one such operation. They automate parts of it, and they differ in which pillars they supply and in how much of the layout they decide for you. | Approach | Supplies | Leaves to you | Suits | |---|---|---|---| | By hand | Whatever you choose, as above | Every step, and its consistency across projects | Learning the pillars; a single paper | | `rrtools` [@marwick2018packaging] | Package-style layout, a Dockerfile, a README | The lockfile, matching the Dockerfile to it, the data manifest | A paper with code, in the community-standard layout | | `workflowr` [@blischak2019workflowr] | A project website in which each results page records its Git commit and R session information | The lockfile, the container, the data manifest | An analysis that is shared as it develops, as a website | | `zzcollab` (@sec-zzcollab-optional) | Layout, `renv.lock`, `.Rprofile`, Dockerfile, a `Makefile`, dependency checks | The data manifest's upkeep, and the choice of profile | A group producing many projects that should look alike | : Ways to assemble a compendium. None removes the audit. {#tbl-zzcollab-approaches} The right level of infrastructure is itself a judgment. Excessive infrastructure on a small project is busywork; insufficient infrastructure on a large one is technical debt. A compendium is overkill for interactive exploration, for a one-off script, for a teaching example whose point is the code, and for a quick reproduction of someone else's analysis, whose structure should control. It is the right weight for a collaborative analysis passed between team members, for one that must survive months or years after its lead analyst has moved on, and for any analysis subject to the federal requirements of @sec-federal. A tool that makes the heavy path cheap moves the right answer toward more infrastructure on the margin, but never removes the need to decide. Whichever path you take, the group's conventions (a preferred database client, a set of in-house packages, a journal's Quarto template) are best written down once, in a template project or a shared lockfile, so that every new project inherits them rather than re-enumerating them. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** A colleague argues that adopting a framework makes the pillar audit unnecessary, since the framework writes every file. What is wrong with the argument? **Answer.** A framework writes the pillars once, at scaffolding time; the audit checks them now. Lockfiles drift as packages are installed, a Dockerfile's base tag falls behind a lockfile snapshotted under a newer R, and data change after the manifest is written. Each failure in @tbl-five-pillars can occur in a scaffolded project as easily as in a hand-built one. ::: ### Exercises 6. For each project below, choose an approach from @tbl-zzcollab-approaches and name the pillar you would check most often: (a) a one-off descriptive table for a clinician's abstract; (b) a two-year trial analysis passed between three analysts; (c) a methods paper with a simulation study. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} (a) A script, with no compendium; if the abstract becomes a paper, promote it then. (b) A framework that makes every project in the group look alike, `zzcollab` or a group template, with the data pillar checked most often, because extracts arrive throughout the trial. (c) `rrtools` or a hand-built compendium; the pillar to watch is the environment (Dockerfile and lockfile together), because simulation results depend on the random-number generator and numerical libraries. Other defensible answers exist; the reasoning should tie the approach to the project's lifetime and number of hands. ::: ## Optional: automating the assembly with zzcollab {#sec-zzcollab-optional} This section is optional. `zzcollab` is the author's in-house framework (@sec-lab-software), one way to automate the assembly beside `rrtools` and `workflowr`; nothing else in the book depends on it. It packages the ideas of `rrtools`, `renv`, and Docker into one command-line workflow, trading control over the layout for speed of setup and uniformity across a group's projects. It does not call `rrtools`; it writes its own layout, modeled on the same compendium.[^zzcollab-version] [^zzcollab-version]: Described as of the repository at `github.com/rgt47/zzcollab` in October 2026. Profiles, `make` targets, and the bundle schema have changed between versions; check the repository's `CHANGELOG.md` and `make help` before relying on the details below. ### The first-project walkthrough The minimum `zzcollab` session (display-only): ```bash mkdir hfhome-analysis cd hfhome-analysis zzc tidyverse # scaffold (Five Pillars appear) make r # enter R session inside Docker # ... do analysis ... make check-renv # validate dependencies make docker-render-qmd # render the Quarto report ``` **`zzc tidyverse`** runs the framework's scaffolding. After it completes, the directory contains a `DESCRIPTION`, `R/`, `analysis/`, and `tests/` directories, a Quarto report at `analysis/report/index.qmd`, a minimal `renv.lock`, a `Dockerfile` on the `rocker/tidyverse` base, and a `Makefile`. It then offers to build the image. Git is a separate step (`zzc git`, or `git init` yourself). The generated Dockerfile pins the rocker base image by tag and, when Docker can resolve it, by digest (for example `rocker/r-ver:4.6.0@sha256:...`). **`make r`** drops you into an interactive R session inside the container, with the project directory mounted, so files edited inside the container persist on the host. It does not build the image; if no image exists it says so and falls back to R on the host. Build first with `make docker-build` if you declined at scaffolding time. **`make check-renv`** runs `zzrenvcheck::check_packages(auto_fix = TRUE, strict = TRUE)` on the host. It checks that the packages your code uses, the packages `DESCRIPTION` declares, and the packages `renv.lock` records all agree, and with `auto_fix` it *edits* `DESCRIPTION` and `renv.lock` to add what is missing. It is not a read-only audit; use `make check-renv-no-fix` for a report that changes nothing. It does not build the Dockerfile or inspect `.Rprofile` or the data. **`make docker-render-qmd`** runs `quarto render analysis/report/index.qmd` inside the container. (`make docker-render` renders an R Markdown report instead, `analysis/report/report.Rmd` by default.) ### The project `Makefile` Every `zzcollab` project gets a `Makefile` with many targets; `make help` lists them. The ones used most: | Target | Action | |---|---| | `make help` | List all targets | | `make r` | Drop into R inside the project's container | | `make rstudio` | Launch RStudio Server (port 8787) | | `make docker-render-qmd` | Render `analysis/report/index.qmd` in the container | | `make check-renv` | Validate dependencies and add missing ones | | `make check-renv-no-fix` | Validate dependencies without modifying files | | `make snapshot` | Snapshot `renv.lock` in the container, then validate | | `make docker-build` | Rebuild the image (use after adding packages) | | `make hash-data` | Write a SHA-256 manifest of the raw-data directory | | `make verify-data` | Check the raw data against that manifest | | `make clean` | Remove package build artifacts | : Common `zzcollab` `make` targets. {#tbl-zzcollab-make} `make hash-data` writes `data-manifest.sha256` in the same `shasum` format as the manifest in @sec-zzcollab-audit, so `audit_pillars()` reads either. `make docker-build` rebuilds the image after you add packages or system dependencies; `make r` silently uses the old image until you do. `make clean` removes package build artifacts (`*.tar.gz` and `*.Rcheck`); it does not touch rendered reports or Quarto's `_freeze/` directory. `make rstudio` is for browser-based work. Open `http://localhost:8787` and log in as `rstudio` with the password `rstudio`, which the target prints. The target publishes port 8787 on all of your machine's network interfaces, so with that fixed password, use it only on a trusted network (see @sec-docker for binding to `127.0.0.1` instead). ### Choosing a profile The command `zzc `, run inside an empty project directory, scaffolds a project using one of four profiles, and a profile's main job is to choose the rocker base image: | Profile | Base image | Approximate size | Use | |---|---|---|---| | `minimal` | `rocker/r-ver` | 650 MB | Command-line work, continuous integration | | `tidyverse` | `rocker/tidyverse` | 1.2 GB | Tidyverse data analysis | | `rstudio` | `rocker/rstudio` | 980 MB | RStudio Server development | | `publishing` | `rocker/verse` | 4.2 GB | Manuscripts that need LaTeX | : `zzcollab` profiles. {#tbl-zzcollab-profiles} The `tidyverse` profile was formerly called `analysis`, and `zzc analysis` still works as a deprecated alias. There are no modeling or Shiny profiles; for those needs the framework's own advice is to start from one of the four and add packages inside the container. The profile is a substantive choice: a manuscript that must render to PDF needs LaTeX, which only the `publishing` profile's base image has, while a simple descriptive analysis in the `publishing` profile waits for a 4 GB image it does not need. Modeling packages need no special profile. Install `lme4` or `survival` inside the container, record them with `make snapshot`, and rebuild with `make docker-build`. When zzcollab generates the Dockerfile it reads the packages your code, `DESCRIPTION`, and `renv.lock` mention and adds the system libraries they need, so a profile mismatch costs a rebuild rather than a hand-edited `apt-get` line. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** You are scaffolding a project that will fit a Cox proportional hazards model with `survival::coxph()` and a mixed-effects model with `lme4::glmer()`, then render the result as a PDF manuscript. Which profile? **Answer.** `publishing`, because the PDF manuscript is the one requirement a profile actually supplies: it is the only profile whose base image includes LaTeX. The modeling packages are not a profile question at all. Install `lme4` and `survival` inside the container, run `make snapshot` so that `renv.lock` and `DESCRIPTION` record them, and rebuild. Neither package needs an extra system library; `survival` is a recommended package that ships with R. ::: ### Bundles and extension Profiles are defined in the repository's `templates/bundles.yaml`, which has three sections: `library_bundles` name sets of system packages, `package_bundles` name sets of R packages, and `profiles` combine a base image with one bundle of each. There is no `inherits` key, and the quickstart command accepts only the four built-in profile names. A group that wants different defaults can add a profile entry in a fork and select it with `zzc docker --profile `, but the Dockerfile generator reads only the entry's `base_image`; system libraries come from the packages the project uses, and R packages are added inside the container and recorded with `make snapshot`. Group conventions therefore belong in a template project or a shared `renv.lock`, as for any other approach, not in a new profile. ### Exercises 7. Scaffold a `zzcollab` project in a scratch directory, copy the two HF-HOME files into `analysis/data/raw_data/`, run `make hash-data`, and audit the result with `audit_pillars()`. (This needs Docker and the `zzc` command, and creates a project on your machine.) ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} A complete scaffold passes every row except, until you commit, the source-code row's Git check (`zzc git` or `git init`). If the Dockerfile row fails, compare its `FROM` line with the lockfile's `R$Version`: the two were written at different times, and the fix is to rebuild with `make docker-build` after a snapshot, not to edit the tag by hand. Run `make check-renv-no-fix` as well; unlike `make check-renv`, it changes nothing. ::: ## Rules of thumb 1. **Habit 1: the compendium is the unit.** Code, data, environment, and paper travel together in one directory with a convention a stranger knows; audit all five pillars, not the ones a tool happens to write, and tag what you submit, because the fresh clone of that tag is the test. 2. **Habit 2: raw data are evidence; derived data are a build product.** Never write to `raw_data/`, commit a checksum manifest and change it only when new data arrive deliberately, and regenerate everything else from code. 3. **Habit 4: pin the environment.** The lockfile and the Dockerfile pin different layers, and they must agree on the R version. ## Cumulative practice 8. *Cumulative (uses @sec-git-solo, @sec-quarto, @sec-renv, and @sec-docker).* Assemble by hand a compendium for a small HF-HOME analysis: the `rrtools` layout, with `randomization.csv` and `outcomes.csv` in `analysis/data/raw_data/` and a checksum manifest; a `paper.qmd` that reports the 30-day event proportion in each arm with inline code; `renv` with a snapshot; and the canonical Dockerfile with its tag set from the lockfile. Commit and tag `v0.1`. Run `audit_pillars()` until every row passes, then build the image and render the paper inside it from a fresh clone. 9. *On your own work (no key).* Convert a 'scripts and data' project of your own into a compendium, documenting the location of every file and the reason for it. Audit it with `audit_pillars()`, record for each failing pillar what it would take to close it and whether you think it is worth it, and record what the fresh-clone check found the first time you ran it. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} 8. The paper's numbers come from the raw files, never typed. A minimal computing chunk: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} rand <- read.csv(file.path(raw_dir, "randomization.csv"), colClasses = c(patient_id = "character")) outc <- read.csv(file.path(hf_dir, "outcomes.csv"), colClasses = c(patient_id = "character")) hf <- merge(rand[c("patient_id", "arm")], outc[c("patient_id", "event_30d")], by = "patient_id") stopifnot(nrow(hf) == nrow(rand)) round(100 * tapply(hf$event_30d, hf$arm, mean, na.rm = TRUE), 1) #> Home health Usual care #> 21.1 23.7 ``` ::: The chunk reads `outcomes.csv` from the HF-HOME directory, because the Pitfall in @sec-rrtools-layout edited the toy compendium's copy; in your compendium, both files come from `raw_data/`, and `check_raw()` runs first. If the audit's Dockerfile row fails, the base tag and the lockfile's R version disagree; set the tag from `renv::lockfile_read("renv.lock")$R$Version`. A passing audit is still a structural check; the fresh-clone render is the test. ::: ## Cheat sheet | Task | Command or file | Guards against | |---|---|---| | Scaffold a compendium | `rrtools::use_compendium()`, `use_analysis()` | An improvised layout | | Pin what is beneath R | The canonical Dockerfile (@sec-docker-canonical); base tag equals `renv::lockfile_read("renv.lock")$R$Version` | A different R or system library | | Pin the packages | `renv::init()`, `renv::snapshot()`; check with `renv::status()` | Newer packages on a collaborator's machine | | Activate the project library | `.Rprofile`, written by `renv::init()`; check `.libPaths()[1]` from the render directory | A lockfile silently bypassed | | Protect raw data | `data-manifest.sha256`, from `cli::hash_file_sha256()` or `make hash-data`; `shasum -a 256 --check data-manifest.sha256` | Edits saved over the raw export; a later extract | | Audit the pillars | `audit_pillars(".")`; `git ls-files` | A pillar missing, inert, or not committed | | Render the paper | `quarto render analysis/paper/paper.qmd` | Typed numbers | | Use a journal format | `quarto use template quarto-journals/` | Reformatting by hand | | Test the compendium | Fresh clone, `docker build`, `docker run` | Files that live only on your machine | | Mark a milestone | `git tag -a v1.0-submission` | Not knowing what was submitted | : Compendium tasks at a glance. {#tbl-zzcollab-cheat-sheet} ## Further reading - [@marwick2018packaging], the paper that defines the research compendium as this chapter uses it, and whose framing every approach in the chapter inherits. - [@marwick2018rrtools], the `rrtools` package and its documentation. - [@harrell2025rworkflow], the closest peer treatment of what goes in the compendium's `analysis/` directory once it exists. ## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-10} 1. A research compendium is a directory tree that bundles a study's code, data, and narrative in one place, with a standardized layout. The reader can rerun the analyses and regenerate the paper with a single command. Marwick et al. (2018) argue that the compendium is the appropriate unit of reproducible research in R. An `rrtools` compendium has three components: an R package backbone (`DESCRIPTION`, `R/`), which gives dependency declaration (`Imports:`); an `analysis/` directory for the data and the paper, which holds the study; and a Dockerfile which, with `renv.lock`, gives environment reproducibility. A regular R package exports functions for reuse by others and has no data or narrative; the compendium repurposes the package structure as infrastructure, not for distribution on CRAN. 2. The Five Pillars are: (1) a **Dockerfile** (captures the operating system and system libraries), (2) an **renv.lock** (captures R package versions), (3) an **.Rprofile** (activates renv and sets project-local R options), (4) **source code** (the actual analysis), and (5) **data** (raw and processed, or a documented access path when data cannot be shared). Each pillar captures a layer that the others do not, and removing any one leaves the analysis unreproducible. A project with only a committed `renv.lock` and a Dockerfile still has to pin the source code and the data (and, if it has no `.Rprofile`, its activation). The code is pinned when it is committed and the reported version tagged; the data, when the files are in the repository or a committed checksum manifest records them. Nobody notices their absence until a rerun gives a different answer, which is why the audit in @sec-zzcollab-audit checks for them explicitly. 3. A framework is worth adopting when many projects should look alike or the setup will be repeated often; for a single paper, assembling by hand or with `rrtools` is enough. Every framework writes the pillars once. Keeping them consistent afterwards (lockfile, Dockerfile tag, data manifest) is still yours, and the audit is how you check it. `zzcollab` *wraps* `renv` and Docker and *follows* `rrtools`'s layout without calling it.
